video_title: Could Treasury Yields Break the AI Boom?
gist: Jesse Felder argues a slow-motion sovereign debt crisis (led by Japan but spreading to the US and UK) is colliding with a fiscal and AI-capex borrowing binge to push the 10-year Treasury yield higher, and that the July blow-off in leveraged AI/semiconductor trades (South Korean retail, the Situational Awareness hedge fund) marked the final speculative capitulation of the AI bubble, whose next catalyst to watch is whether OpenAI and Anthropic can actually IPO to fund their compute commitments.

insights.claim: Jesse Felder treats the 10-year Treasury yield as the single most important chart in markets because, as the risk-free rate, it is the discount rate underlying every other asset price.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Investors should treat the 10-year yield as the master variable driving equity valuations, AI financing costs, and gold/commodity pricing simultaneously, not a siloed rates story.
insights.quote: the 10-year Treasury yield is the most important chart in the world because it's the risk-free rate of return

insights.claim: Felder cites the Taylor Rule as implying the Fed funds rate should be over 6% given nominal GDP growth that annualized above 7% last quarter, versus an actual policy rate of roughly 3.5-3.75%, meaning the Fed is running about 300 basis points behind the curve.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: A Fed this far behind a policy rule while GDP runs hot argues for continued upward pressure on long-end yields rather than an imminent dovish pivot.
insights.quote: Taylor rule says that the Fed is behind the curve by as much as 300 basis points

insights.claim: Felder uses gold as a leading indicator: strength in gold over the past 18-24 months has been leading the broader commodity complex, which in turn is a leading indicator for interest rates.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: A reusable cross-asset framework: rising gold today can be read as an early warning for higher commodity prices and higher yields months later.

insights.claim: Felder's core macro thesis is that a slow-motion debt crisis is unfolding across all major developed sovereign bond markets, not just Japan, and that it directly threatens both equity valuations and financing for the AI buildout.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Frame the Japan currency/bond stress not as an isolated story but as a template for what could hit US and UK long-end yields next, with direct read-through to AI-infrastructure financing costs.
insights.quote: I do believe we're watching kind of a slow motion debt crisis unfold

insights.claim: Citing Robin Brooks' framework relating sovereign debt-to-GDP to long-term yields, Felder argues Japan's yields (2-3% on 10-30 year bonds against debt/GDP over 200%) are mispriced by at least 100-200 basis points and should arguably be 5-7%.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: If Japanese long-end yields normalize toward this fair-value estimate, it implies a large repricing event with global spillover, not a contained local issue.
insights.quote: they could have five six 7% on the long end and you know they're at two 3% from you know 10 to 30 year bonds

insights.claim: Felder describes a direct transmission mechanism: yen weakness forces Japan to intervene by selling US Treasuries to buy yen, which pushes US yields up and, combined with a Fed chair unwilling to define a clear reaction function, is drawing out 'bond vigilantes' simultaneously in the US, Japan and the UK.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Japanese currency intervention is a real, mechanical channel pushing US yields higher right now, and it can recur as long as the yen stays under pressure.

insights.claim: Felder frames Kevin Warsh's removal of forward guidance as an attempt to strip the moral hazard created by promises like 'rates will stay at zero indefinitely,' citing Silicon Valley Bank's purchase of long-duration bonds at low rates based on the Fed's forward guidance as the cautionary example of that moral hazard.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: A less-promise-driven Fed regime should reduce reflexive risk-taking (e.g., banks/speculators betting on rate paths), which is healthy but also removes a source of market certainty investors had priced in.
insights.quote: Fed's going to keep interest rates low. They're going to try and look through this inflation problem, calling it transitory, so we're going to go ahead and and buy a bunch of these long-term bonds at low too low of interest rates

insights.claim: Felder argues the market's real problem with Warsh isn't removing forward guidance itself but his unwillingness to clarify the Fed's reaction function (what data or inflation measure would trigger a policy response), which undermines confidence the Fed will address inflation if it re-accelerates.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Watch for any Fed communication clarifying its reaction function as a signal that could calm bond vigilantes; continued ambiguity is a reason for yields to keep drifting higher.

insights.claim: Felder argues 2022's monetary tightening barely dented financial conditions, and that genuinely bringing inflation under control requires a much larger tightening this time -- meaningfully lower stock prices and wider high-yield spreads -- effectively recession-like stress in markets.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Investors betting the Fed can tame inflation without a real equity drawdown or credit-spread widening are likely to be disappointed; position for financial-conditions tightening well beyond the 2022 episode.
insights.quote: the Fed needs to be willing to create a tightening in financial conditions that was much more significant than what we saw in 2022

themes.theme: Fiscal & AI Capex Supply Glut Meeting the Bond Market

insights.claim: Felder notes the US is running roughly a 6%-of-GDP fiscal deficit during an economic expansion with low unemployment -- a combination without modern precedent -- generating about $2 trillion a year of new Treasury supply that the market has to absorb.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Structural oversupply of Treasuries during an expansion is itself a source of upward yield pressure independent of Fed policy, arguing for a persistently steeper/higher long end.
insights.quote: that's a $2 trillion uh a year of new supply that needs to come into the market right now

insights.claim: Felder connects AI capex directly to the bond market: hyperscalers have flipped from cash-generative companies that bought back stock to companies spending all their cash flow and then borrowing several hundred billion dollars more, adding fresh supply into an already saturated debt market.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: AI infrastructure spending is not just an equity-multiple story -- it is now a meaningful new source of bond supply that competes with Treasury issuance and can itself push yields higher, tightening financing conditions for the AI buildout in a feedback loop.
insights.quote: now we need another few hundred billion dollars of borrowing on top of that in order to go spend

insights.claim: Felder says the specific trigger he watches is the 10-year and 30-year Treasury yields breaking out to new highs, though he stresses that the level matters less than the volatility of rates.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Watch for the 10-year and 30-year making new highs (rather than just higher absolute levels) as the near-term risk signal for equities and AI financing costs.
insights.quote: breaking out on the 10-year to new highs would I think really start to to worry worry the market

insights.claim: Felder links the MOVE index (Treasury market volatility) closely to stock market correlations, arguing today's unusually low stock correlations (offsetting huge single-stock moves in Microsoft, Google, Nvidia, memory names) are a byproduct of low bond volatility, and rising bond volatility would push stock correlations up.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: A market priced for very low stock-to-stock correlation is vulnerable if bond volatility rises -- that would compress the dispersion that has cushioned the index level even as individual mega-cap names swing 10-15% in a day.
insights.quote: the move index which is the volatility of the treasury market it's very closely related to correlations in the stock market

themes.theme: AI Bubble: Signs of a Blow-off Top

insights.claim: Felder points to Oracle and SpaceX as canaries in the coal mine for the AI trade, noting SpaceX's roughly $700 billion market-cap loss in a single month is, in his description, the single greatest market-cap loss in US stock market history.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Losses of this magnitude in AI-linked names most exposed to speculative capital are an early signal that AI-trade sentiment has turned, ahead of broader index weakness.
insights.quote: SpaceX has just lost 700 billion dollars in market cap in a month, the the the single greatest market cap loss in the history of the US stock market

insights.claim: Using Peter Atwater's framing that bubbles are a 'last in, first out' (LEO) phenomenon, Felder points to South Korean retail traders using leveraged ETFs to pile into semiconductor stocks (illustrated by a story of a 24-year-old trader joking about selling underwear to fund more purchases) as the last, most reckless capital into the AI/semi mania, and the first to blow up.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: The most levered, latest-arriving retail capital in a mania is the leading indicator for a top; its unwind (as with South Korean leveraged semiconductor ETFs) tends to precede broader deleveraging.
insights.quote: bubbles are a last in first out a leo phenomenon

insights.claim: Felder details the collapse of the hedge fund 'Situational Awareness,' whose meme-stock-like manager ran a roughly 4x-leveraged momentum pairs trade -- long AI hardware stocks on the theory they could only go up, short software on the theory it would go bankrupt -- that blew up within a month.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: A concrete, named example of leveraged AI-momentum capital being forcibly unwound, evidence the speculative excess has already started deleveraging rather than merely being a risk on the horizon.
insights.quote: this mindset of buy all of the the AI hardware stocks because they're they can only just go up forever and short software because software companies are going to go bankrupt

insights.claim: Felder's highest-conviction call in the interview is that the July blow-up of the Korean leveraged trade and the Situational Awareness hedge fund marked the final speculative capitulation ('greatest fools') of the AI bubble, and that this is the beginning of the end for the trade.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: A named, dated marker (July's leveraged blow-ups) that an experienced macro analyst is calling the top of the AI speculative cycle -- worth tracking against subsequent price action as a falsifiable call.
insights.quote: I really do think that was the final blowoff of this AI bubble

insights.claim: Felder argues the marginal, highly levered buyers who drove the AI/semiconductor rally -- Korean retail, crypto traders rotating out of Bitcoin, and 4x-levered momentum funds -- are now financially impaired and unlikely to return at the same size, removing a key source of incremental demand for AI-linked stocks.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Even if sentiment stabilizes, the specific capital that powered the recent AI-stock melt-up is capital-impaired, implying weaker forward demand and a harder path back to prior highs for the most speculative AI names.
insights.quote: we're not going to have Korean investors come back into the market. You're not going to have crypto bros come back into the market

insights.claim: Felder says hyperscaler earnings quality has deteriorated to the worst on record -- reported earnings are diverging sharply from free cash flow, which is negative -- partly because prior-quarter gains from marking up stakes in Anthropic and SpaceX are now reversing into losses given SpaceX's subsequent market-cap collapse.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Headline hyperscaler 'earnings beats' are increasingly non-cash and reliant on one-time mark-to-market gains that are now reversing; investors should look through GAAP earnings to free cash flow when judging the health of AI-capex spenders.
insights.quote: these companies have literally never reported lower quality earnings than they are today

insights.claim: Felder argues the recent break in the momentum factor -- one of the largest in history following one of the largest momentum surges ever -- is climactic and echoes the dot-com bust, when value stocks performed phenomenally from March to December 2000 after momentum broke; he already sees early rotation signs (staples over discretionary, software over semis, defensives over cyclicals) and is finding value in beaten-down software names.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: If the momentum-to-value rotation follows the 2000 template, defensive/value sectors and unloved software names could outperform even as AI-momentum leaders continue to struggle -- a concrete relative-value trade Felder says he is already positioning into.
insights.quote: what did well literally from March of 2000 through the end of 2000 was value stocks did phenomenally well

themes.theme: Circular AI Financing and the IPO Trigger

insights.claim: Felder identifies whether OpenAI and Anthropic can successfully IPO as the single most important AI-bubble signpost, because both companies are deeply loss-making and need public equity capital to fund hundreds of billions of dollars in compute commitments to hyperscalers; doubt about Anthropic's ability to go public would be a major warning sign for the entire data-center buildout.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Track OpenAI and Anthropic IPO progress as a leading indicator: a stalled or failed IPO process would signal the AI capex supercycle is running out of funding, with direct read-through to hyperscaler capex and AI-linked equities.
insights.quote: if you start to see doubt about anthropic being able to come public, that's going to be a huge warning sign as to the sustainability of what's going on with the data center data center buildout

insights.claim: Felder cites Amazon giving OpenAI $35 billion well ahead of schedule -- despite the funding being contractually contingent on an AI breakthrough or an OpenAI IPO, neither of which had occurred -- as evidence of circular AI financing that he expects to unwind; Anthropic is targeting an IPO within a couple of months, while OpenAI's is not expected until next year.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Hyperscalers are already funding AI labs' ability to pay them back for compute, a circular arrangement Felder flags as unsustainable; a breakdown here would be a direct hit to reported hyperscaler AI revenue.
insights.quote: We'll give you the 35 billion anyways because you have to have the money to pay us for the, you know, for the compute

insights.claim: Felder says gold overshot its real-rate-implied fair value earlier this year, has since corrected back in line with rising real rates (a headwind for gold), and expects further Fed hikes over the next six to nine months to keep gold pressured short-term -- though gold should pre-emptively start pricing the next dovish pivot; he trimmed his long-standing gold overweight (held since 2016) when it looked overvalued and has since added back some exposure now that it is closer to fair value.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Expect gold to stay range-bound/consolidating through further Fed hikes rather than immediately resuming its uptrend; the next major gold rally likely requires visible evidence the Fed is turning dovish again.
insights.quote: the Fed may be facing a series of rate hikes over the next six to nine, you know, months or so

insights.claim: Felder argues oil is historically cheap relative to gold and silver -- cheaper than it has ever been on that relative basis -- despite performing as well as the tech sector over the past five years, and sees fundamental fair value well over $100 a barrel, making energy the most attractive sector in the current commodities bull market, itself driven by a structural (not cyclical) shift away from the pre-pandemic disinflationary regime of globalization and favorable demographics.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: A specific, high-conviction relative-value commodity call: oil/energy as the cheapest way to play a structurally higher-inflation regime, with an explicit price target of well over $100/barrel.
insights.quote: oil has never been as cheap relative to the gold price or the silver price as it is today

insights.claim: Felder points to Warren Buffett holding roughly $400 billion in short-term Treasuries as validation for hiding out in cash/short-duration instruments while the debt-crisis and AI-bubble risks he describes play out.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: A well-known, high-profile allocator's cash stockpile is offered as a simple, low-complexity playbook for investors wanting to de-risk ahead of a potential yield spike or equity correction: short-duration Treasuries over risk assets.
insights.quote: Warren Buffett has 400 billion in short-term treasuries right now
